statement: In adults who smoked and joined four small randomised trials of oral nicotine pouches (284 people; 7 days to 8 weeks; three of the four trials enrolled people not planning to quit; Cochrane review, search to 13 January 2025, with ten further trials ongoing), the evidence is insufficient to say whether pouches help people stop smoking or cut down, whether compared with continuing to smoke, with a nicotine e-cigarette or with a lower-strength pouch. Compared with continuing to smoke as usual, 1 of 18 people given pouches had quit at week 8 against 0 of 9 (risk ratio 1.58, 95% CI 0.07 to 35.32; one trial, 27 people; very low certainty); among people still smoking, cigarettes per day differed by −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58; 19 people). Compared with a nicotine e-cigarette (the same trial of 45 people, at high risk of bias), 1 of 18 had quit with pouches against 4 of 18 with e-cigarettes (0.25, 0.03 to 2.02; 36 people; low certainty), and people still smoking smoked 5.32 more cigarettes a day with pouches (−2.16 to 12.80; 26 people). Between two pouch strengths (one registry-listed trial), 2 of 15 had quit at the higher strength against 0 of 15 at the lower at week 4 (5.00, 0.26 to 96.13; 30 people). None of these differences can be told from chance. No trial compared pouches with nicotine replacement for quitting (one cross-over trial of 63 people reported side effects only), none followed people beyond 8 weeks, none included people who vape or use other products, and the review found no study of pouch uptake and smoking in the population. No serious adverse events were recorded in any arm of the three trials that reported them (1 to 8 weeks; very low to low certainty); other adverse events were reported in different ways and were mostly mild or uncommon. In the one trial funded by a tobacco company (53 people, about one week), urine and blood measures of smoke exposure were lower with pouches than with continued smoking (a tobacco-specific nitrosamine marker, NNAL, 265 ng/g creatinine lower, 95% CI 180 to 351, from 330; carboxyhaemoglobin 6.7 percentage points lower, 5.1 to 8.3, from 11.3%; very low certainty); it is the only trial in the review to measure those two against continued smoking, and an independent trial of 19 people that measured exhaled carbon monoxide found it lower with pouches, with an interval that included no difference. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Only four small trials have tested nicotine pouches in people who smoke: 284 people in all, followed for 1 to 8 weeks. They are too small to say whether pouches help people stop smoking or cut down. In the one trial that reported quitting against carrying on smoking, 1 of 18 people given pouches had stopped and none of 9 who carried on; and 1 of 18 given pouches had stopped against 4 of 18 given vapes. No serious health problems were recorded, but the trials were short. One trial paid for by a tobacco company found lower levels of smoke chemicals in the body after about a week of pouches than after smoking as usual; it was the only trial to measure these, so nothing independent can be set beside it. Ten more trials are under way.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined four small randomised trials of oral nicotine pouches (284 people; 7 days to 8 weeks; three trials enrolled people not planning to quit); Cochrane review, search to 13 January 2025; ten further trials ongoing
exposure: Oral nicotine pouches given by the trial
comparator: Continuing to smoke as usual; a nicotine e-cigarette; a lower-strength pouch (and, for side effects only, snus and nicotine gum)
outcome: Not smoking at week 8 (week 4 in one trial); cigarettes per day in people still smoking; serious and other adverse events; NNAL and carboxyhaemoglobin after about a week
magnitude: Quitting (RR; events; participants): pouch vs continued smoking at week 8, 1/18 vs 0/9, RR 1.58 (95% CI 0.07–35.32), 1 trial, 27, very low certainty; pouch vs nicotine e-cigarette at week 8, 1/18 vs 4/18, RR 0.25 (0.03–2.02), 1 trial, 36, low certainty (review's table: 222 per 1,000 with e-cigarettes vs 56 per 1,000 with pouches; about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate, editors' subtraction); higher vs lower strength at week 4, 2/15 vs 0/15, RR 5.00 (0.26–96.13), 1 trial, 30, not graded. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: vs continued smoking MD −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58), 19; vs e-cigarette MD 5.32 (−2.16 to 12.80), 26; higher vs lower strength, log scale MD −0.20 (−0.27 to −0.13), 30. Serious adverse events: none in any arm (3 trials; vs continued smoking 2 trials, 124 participants, very low; vs e-cigarette 1 trial, 26, low; higher vs lower strength 2 trials, 77). Biomarkers vs continued smoking (Rensch 2023, industry-funded, 53 participants): NNAL MD −265.30 ng/g creatinine (−350.64 to −179.96), COHb MD −6.7% (−8.33 to −5.07); very low.

evidence.locator: Results › Included studies, Table 4 (overview), Participants, Interventions and comparators; Results of the search
evidence.extracted: Four randomised trials, 284 participants: Avila 2024 (USA, 45 people: pouch, e-cigarette, no intervention); Caldwell 2010 (New Zealand, 63, cross-over of pouch, snus and nicotine gum, adverse events only); NCT04250727 (USA, 30: higher against lower strength, registry record only); Rensch 2023 (USA, 146, tobacco-industry funded: pouches of three strengths against a no-tobacco group and a continue-smoking group). All enrolled adults who smoked; three enrolled people not planning to quit; follow-up 7 days to 8 weeks. Ten ongoing trials are listed.

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus minimal control › Smoking behaviour, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary of findings 1, row 1 and footnotes a and b
evidence.extracted: Pouch against minimal control, abstinence at week 8: 1 of 18 given pouches had quit against 0 of 9 with no intervention; RR 1.58 (0.07 to 35.32), 1 trial, 27 participants (Avila 2024, high risk of bias); very low certainty (two levels for risk of bias and two for imprecision). The table's 11 per 1,000 and 18 per 1,000 come from a zero-event correction, not observed rates. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking at week 8: mean difference −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58), 19 people with complete data.

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus e-cigarettes › Smoking behaviour and Biomarkers; Summary of findings 3
evidence.extracted: Pouch against e-cigarette (nicotine pods), abstinence at week 8: 1 of 18 quit with pouches against 4 of 18 with e-cigarettes; RR 0.25 (0.03 to 2.02), 1 trial, 36 participants; the table gives 222 per 1,000 with e-cigarettes against 56 per 1,000 (7 to 449) with pouches (editors' subtraction: about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate). Low certainty (two levels for imprecision; 5 events in all); not downgraded for risk of bias because both arms were equally intensive although unblinded. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: MD 5.32 (−2.16 to 12.80), 26 people with complete data; exhaled carbon monoxide higher with pouches, interval including no difference.

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Smoking behaviour and Adverse events; Table 5 (NCT04250727)
evidence.extracted: Higher against lower strength pouch (NCT04250727; registry record, unclear risk of bias), abstinence at week 4: 2 of 15 quit at the higher strength against 0 of 15 at the lower; RR 5.00 (0.26 to 96.13), 30 participants; certainty not assessed (a dose comparison was not a planned summary-of-findings comparison). Cigarettes per day (log scale) lower with the higher strength: MD −0.20 (−0.27 to −0.13), n = 30. Any adverse event 13 of 15 in each arm; two participants in the higher-strength arm reported nicotine toxicity symptoms during dual use of cigarettes and pouches.

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events (ONP against minimal control; ONP versus e-cigarettes; ONP at different doses); Summary of findings 1 and 3; Plain language summary › What did we find?
evidence.extracted: Serious adverse events: none in any arm in the trials reporting them. Against minimal control, 2 trials (Avila 2024; Rensch 2023), 124 participants, very low certainty (two levels for risk of bias, two for imprecision); against e-cigarettes, 1 trial, 26 participants, low certainty (imprecision); higher against lower strength, NCT04250727 and Rensch 2023, 77 participants; Rensch 2023 against a no-tobacco group, none. Follow-up 1 to 8 weeks. The authors conclude it is unclear whether pouches change the chance of a serious event.

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events; ONP versus snus; ONP versus nicotine replacement therapy; Table 5
evidence.extracted: Other adverse events (not pooled): cough and shortness of breath were more frequent with pouches than with e-cigarettes in the first week of Avila 2024 (cough 5 against 3, breathlessness 6 against 1 people) and similar by week 4; Rensch 2023 reported 86 events in 56 of 146 people (38%), 76 mild and 10 moderate, headache most frequent, 4 judged related to the product, not split by arm; Caldwell 2010 (63 people, cross-over, rating scales) found side effects uncommon for pouch, snus and gum, with fewer reports of bad taste with pouches than with snus or gum.

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus minimal control › Biomarkers; ONP versus no tobacco or nicotine product use › Biomarkers; Summary of findings 1, rows 3 and 4
evidence.extracted: Biomarkers against minimal control (Rensch 2023, tobacco-industry funded, high risk of bias, 53 people, about one week): NNAL mean difference −265.30 ng/g creatinine (−350.64 to −179.96) from a control mean of 330; COHb −6.7% (−8.33 to −5.07) from a control mean of 11.3%; 16 further urinary biomarkers all favoured pouches with intervals excluding no difference. Very low certainty (risk of bias, imprecision). Against a no-tobacco group (46 people) none of 18 biomarkers clearly differed. Avila 2024 (19 people) found lower exhaled carbon monoxide with pouches than continued smoking, interval including no difference.

evidence.locator: Results › Description of studies › Outcomes; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review; Authors' conclusions
evidence.extracted: Gaps stated by the review: no study of prevalence of smoking or other nicotine use; no data on pouches for stopping or cutting down vaping, heated tobacco, snus or other products (all participants smoked); no data on metals or inflammatory markers; no trial with follow-up beyond 8 weeks; no abstinence result for the comparison with nicotine replacement; at most two studies in any analysis, so serious imprecision for every outcome; ten ongoing studies; industry reports were not searched; evidence reaches January 2025.

evidence.locator: Results › Included studies › Funding; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 2nd paragraph; Sources of support; Declarations of interest
evidence.extracted: Rensch 2023 was funded by the pouch manufacturer (a tobacco company); the other three trials by philanthropic, academic or governmental bodies. The industry trial reported no smoking outcome, no serious events, and the largest set of biomarker results. The review was funded by the US National Cancer Institute and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products through CAsToR 3.0; the review says no author took part in an included trial; no author declares funding from a tobacco, pouch or e-cigarette company (some declare payments from smoking-cessation medicine makers and public bodies).

evidence.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 7th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: None of the four trials was at low risk of bias overall: Avila 2024, Caldwell 2010 and Rensch 2023 high, NCT04250727 unclear. Performance bias high in Avila 2024 and Rensch 2023 (unblinded, unequal intervention).

risk_of_bias.note: None of the four trials low risk; three high; unblinded arms, unequal interventions; the comparison with continued smoking rests on one high-risk trial.

indirectness.note: Quitting at 4 to 8 weeks only; three trials enrolled people not planning to quit; all participants smoked.

imprecision.note: Five quits in all across the comparisons; intervals from 0.03 to 96.

publication_bias.note: Ten ongoing trials; industry reports not searched; recorded, not rated.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane systematic review that found no meta-analysis worth pooling (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). Risk of bias, two levels: none of the four trials was at low risk and three were high, with unblinded arms and unequal interventions in the two trials that matter for quitting; the comparison with continued smoking rests on one trial at high risk of bias (the review's two levels). Indirectness, one level: quitting was measured at 4 to 8 weeks, not the 6 months that the claim's question needs, three of the four trials enrolled people not planning to quit, and no trial included people who vape or use other products. Imprecision, two levels: five people had quit across all comparisons, and the risk ratios' intervals run from 0.03 to 96. Inconsistency does not arise (single trials). Publication bias, not rated down but recorded: ten further trials are ongoing and industry reports were not searched. The total of five levels is more than the three available, so the rating is very low; it is not changed by the biomarker result, which is a separate outcome from one tobacco-industry trial (very low), with no independent trial to set beside it. Relation insufficient-evidence (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: the comparison with continued smoking and the comparison with e-cigarettes come from the same trial of 45 people, the higher-against-lower-strength comparison from a registry record of one trial, and the review's plain language summary speaks of two studies behind those comparisons when both come from one trial.

verification.flag_note: The review's search ended in January 2025 with ten ongoing trials, so this claim will be out of date as they report; reader 69's claim cl_nic_pouches covers what pouches contain and who uses them. The claim says plainly that the evidence is thin, as asked. The biomarker finding comes from one tobacco-industry trial with no independent counterpart for those outcomes; it is set in the statement beside that fact, not dropped. Rated very low although the review rates the e-cigarette comparison low: the claim covers the whole question (stopping or cutting down), and its weakest link is the comparison with continued smoking. Not read: the four trial reports, supplementary materials 1 to 6, the flow diagram and risk-of-bias figure (images), the reference list. No new reference is needed (hartmann-boyce_2025 exists).
